system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

output_text:
You were diagnosed with sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis (lung TB that responds to medicines) in 2019 and the disease was noted as active on 07/02/2020. On 03/02/2020 you developed a spontaneous pneumothorax (air‑filled lung collapse) on the right side, so a right chest drainage (tube to remove air) was placed. A pleurostomy (surgical opening in the chest) was done on 03/03/2020 and closed later when the lung collapsed and needed pleural drainage (fluid removal). A Heimlich valve (one‑way valve for drainage) was attached on 10/03 and removed on 27/03, keeping the drain open for the ostomy (continued drainage). A new pleurotomy (another chest opening) was performed on 31/03. Because of bleeding inside tuberculous cavities (areas of infection) you required an emergency exploratory thoracotomy (chest opening to look inside) on 07/04, after which the cavity was packed with compresses (gauze) on the same day. On 11/04/2020 a right pneumonectomy (removal of the whole right lung) was carried out by lateral thoracotomy (side chest opening) together with a tracheostomy (hole in the neck for breathing). Both the chest drain and the tracheostomy tube were removed on 06/06.

During the stay you developed three surgical wound infections caused by multidrug‑resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (hard‑to‑kill bacteria). You were treated with vancomycin (antibiotic to fight infection), meropenem (antibiotic), and amikacin (antibiotic) until 02/04 when the drugs were stopped after you improved and your procalcitonin (infection marker) fell to 0.09. You also had hypovolemic shock (low blood volume causing low pressure) due to wound bleeding from the pleurostomy, which needed urgent surgery on 07/04. On 10/04 you suffered a cardiopulmonary arrest (heart stopped) in asystole (no heart rhythm) for about 4 minutes because of low oxygen (hypoxia).

You were admitted on 03/02/2020 and discharged on 09/05/2020 after a stay of 3 months 6 days 7 hours in a ward bed. The payer was sus. You were referred because you had a persistent dry cough for 4 weeks with night sweats. Three days before admission you had an unmeasured fever with shortness of breath, and one day before admission you felt sudden sharp pain in the right side of the chest that spread to the right neck, together with worsening shortness of breath. You did not cough up blood or sputum. You mentioned being in prison for about 3 years out of a 6‑year term and having been symptom‑free since then. About one month ago you lost roughly 8 kg (weight loss) but did not give exact numbers. You denied any urinary or bowel changes.

On examination you were pale (1/4), hydrated, not blue (acyanotic), not yellow (anictic), conscious and oriented. Your heart rate was 85 beats per minute with normal rhythmic sounds (normal S1 and S2) and no murmurs. Breath sounds were heard in the left chest (vesicular breath sounds) but were absent in the right chest, with uneven chest expansion and no extra noises. Your oxygen saturation (blood oxygen level) was 98 %. The abdomen was flat with normal bowel sounds, soft and not tender. Your limbs had no swelling, no deep‑vein‑thrombosis signs, and good peripheral blood flow. The surgical wound was dry, clean and the stitches were intact.

A sensitivity test for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (TB bacteria) was done on sputum (spit sample) collected on 02/03/2020, reported on 28/02/2020 using DNA hybridization GenoType MTB‑DR plus (test for drug resistance). The test showed sensitivity to rifampin (TB medicine) and isoniazid (TB medicine). A bacilloscopy (microscope test) on sputum collected on 02/03/2020, reported on 02/07/2020 by Ziehl‑Neelsen staining (special stain), was positive with 10 to 99 bacilli per 100 fields.

For follow‑up you will continue treatment with RI (TB regimen) and you have been given a two‑month prescription of oral iron replacement (to treat low iron). A meeting was held with [person] together with the thoracic surgery team, and all doubts about the condition and treatment were clarified. [person] understood the guidelines and thanked the team. You are asked to get the listed examinations for a follow‑up appointment, which is scheduled at [organization] with the thoracic surgery team. You were told the warning signs and instructed to call if any concerns arise. A report and contact details for [organization] were provided for assisted treatment by infectious diseases and thoracic surgery. At discharge you were in good general condition, with no complaints.
